name: model-view-viewmodel
intent: Separate a screen's presentation state and behaviour from the markup that renders it: the view-model exposes view-shaped observable properties and commands, the view binds to them declaratively through the platform's binding engine, and neither side needs a reference to the other.
problem: Presentation logic gets tangled into the view: event handlers and widget objects hold screen state, the same value is duplicated across controls, validation and enablement live in code-behind, and neither the screen's behaviour (untestable without the UI) nor its markup (unchangeable without touching logic) can evolve independently.
context: Markup- or component-driven UI stacks that ship a binding engine - XAML/WPF/MAUI/WinUI, JavaFX/FXML, QML, SwiftUI, Compose, Android Views/LiveData, Vue/Angular - and screens whose state is long-lived enough to own a view-model: forms, editors, dashboards, list/detail navigation, and any screen that must survive a redesign or be tested without launching a UI.
benefits: Presentation state, derived values and commands become unit-testable: a view-model is a plain object with no UI types, so tests exercise exactly the state the screen uses.
The view and the view-model evolve independently - a reskin, a new platform shell or a designer's markup change touches bindings, not presentation logic.
View-shaped state (formatted values, selection, enablement, validation errors) lives in one place instead of being spread across widget event handlers and duplicated between controls.
Two-way binding removes the copy-back code between controls and state, and the binding engine updates only what actually changed.
Roles separate design from development: markup can be authored against a view-model contract, and design-time or sample data substitutes for the live model.
Commands replace ad-hoc event wiring, so invocation, enablement (CanExecute) and parameterisation are expressed once on the view-model.
tradeoffs: Binding is resolved at run time in most stacks: a typo in a binding path, a missing change notification or a broken converter fails silently at run time instead of at compile time.

Change-notification discipline is a correctness burden - every bound property must notify after the value really changed - and getting it subtly wrong (wrong property name, notification mid-update, missed derived property) produces stale UI that no unit test of the view-model sees.
The binding layer itself is untested by view-model tests: converters, command wiring and binding targets only fail in integration, so a second, slower test layer is still required.

Indirection and volume: three roles plus binder, converters and commands are more moving parts than an inline handler, and view-models tend to accrete view concerns (navigation, formatting, focus) until presentation is coupled to one UI again.
Binding has runtime cost and a lifecycle: per-property listeners and large observable collections add overhead, and observers must be detached or they keep views (or whole object graphs) alive.
The pattern presupposes a binder: where the platform has none (plain C without a toolkit, server-rendered web), it must be hand-built or it simply does not pay off.

participants.responsibility: Declarative markup or widget tree that renders the view-model's state and routes user interaction back as bindings and command invocations; holds no business or presentation logic beyond layout and appearance.
View-shaped abstraction of the screen: observable properties (including derived, formatted and validation state) and commands, with change notification; it never references concrete view types.
Domain data and business rules (entities, services, repositories) that the view-model adapts or exposes for binding; unaware of views and view-models.

The platform's binding and notification engine (XAML binding engine, JavaFX properties, QML engine, SwiftUI Observation, LiveData/Compose runtime, Vue/Angular reactivity): observes property changes, transfers values, applies converters and validation.
An invocable action object or method the view calls without knowing what it does; carries its own enablement (CanExecute) and parameter.

use_cases: Data-entry and line-of-business screens (WPF/MAUI/WinUI, JavaFX, Android) where fields validate, depend on each other and must be tested without launching the UI.
Mobile screens that must survive configuration changes or process re-creation: Android ViewModel + StateFlow/LiveData, SwiftUI @Observable models.
Desktop applications with designer-authored markup (QML, FXML, XAML) that must be restyled or re-themed without touching behaviour.
Web and multi-platform SPAs whose screen state must be observable, typed and testable (Vue ref/reactive, Angular signals, MobX observable view-models).
Dashboards and editors where the same state feeds several views or widgets and updates arrive from streams or background work.
Applications ported across platforms while keeping one presentation logic layer (shared view-models over per-platform views).
Cross-platform XAML screens in .NET MAUI: bind XAML controls to a BindingContext view-model with one-way/two-way properties and ICommand actions, so interaction logic stays testable outside the page.
Android Jetpack Compose screens: a screen-level ViewModel exposes one immutable UI state as StateFlow, and composables collect it lifecycle-aware while sending user events back as methods.
SwiftUI screens on Apple platforms: an @Observable model is the source of truth, @State owns its lifetime, and views read tracked properties or create Bindable two-way editors.
avoid_when: Trivial or static screens (about boxes, splash screens, one-shot dialogs): plain markup or a direct widget call is simpler.
Server-rendered request/response stacks, where state is built once per request and rendered: MVC/MVP with presenters or plain templates is the simpler fit.
Immediate-mode or redraw-from-state UIs (egui, Dear ImGui, LVGL with explicit refresh): rendering from a state struct each frame gives the same separation without a binder.
Command-line tools and batch jobs: there is no persistent interactive state to bind.
The platform provides no binding engine and the team will not hand-write one: plain callbacks or a one-way store (Flux/Redux-style) are cheaper.
Screens whose entire state can live in one locally owned component: local state plus an explicit re-render is fewer moving parts than a view-model contract.
anti_patterns: God view-model: navigation, I/O, formatting and domain rules all in one class, so the 'testable presentation layer' becomes the hardest file in the app.
Code-behind comeback: keeping half the logic in markup event handlers or converters while calling the rest MVVM, so behaviour has two homes and neither is tested.
View-model holding view types (Button, TextView, DOM elements) or platform contexts - the pattern's core promise (UI-free testing, replaceable views) is lost.
Notification spam: raising change events on every set, for whole collections, or mid-update, causing cascades, re-entrancy and UI storms.
Two-way binding straight into domain entities, bypassing validation and invariants, so invalid intermediate states are written to the model.
'MVVM' as a folder naming convention: view-models that are only DTOs while all behaviour stays in the view.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: rendering versus presentation state and behaviour.
Single responsibility per role: one view-model owns one screen's (or section's) presentation logic.
Dependency inversion: the view depends on a view-model contract; the view-model depends on model abstractions, never on view types.
Information hiding: the view-model exposes view-shaped state and commands, not the domain model internals.
Testability as a design constraint: if the presentation logic cannot run without a UI, the boundary is wrong.
best_practices: Raise change notifications only when a value really changed, after the object is in a consistent state, and once per property per synchronous operation.
Expose actions as commands with their own enablement instead of toggling control state from code-behind.
Keep view types and platform contexts out of view-models; adapt with converters or formatters at the binding.
Prefer one-way binding plus commands; reserve two-way binding for genuine two-way editors (text fields, toggles) and guard setters against no-op writes.
Keep view-models small and composable per screen or section, with services injected rather than looked up.
Test the view-model without the UI, and keep a thin integration test for the bindings and converters unit tests cannot reach.
Unbind, cancel and dispose observers when a view or screen goes away; treat a binding as an owned resource.
sources: John Gossman, Introduction to Model/View/ViewModel pattern for building WPF apps (8 October 2005) - the pattern's origin: MVC refined for declarative UIs and a general data-binding mechanism; the ViewModel holds view state, data-transformers and commands. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/johngossman/introduction-to-modelviewviewmodel-pattern-for-building-wpf-apps

Josh Smith, Patterns - WPF Apps With The Model-View-ViewModel Design Pattern, MSDN Magazine, February 2009 - the canonical WPF articulation (binding engine, DataContext, templates, ICommand/RelayCommand, ViewModelBase, unit-testability). https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2009/february/patterns-wpf-apps-with-the-model-view-viewmodel-design-pattern

Microsoft Learn, Model-View-ViewModel - .NET: the three components and their interactions, view-first vs view-model-first composition, and the notification rules (raise only on change, at a safe point, never in the constructor). https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/maui/mvvm

Wikipedia, Model-view-viewmodel: the pattern's relationship to Fowler's Presentation Model, the Model-View-Binder alternate name, and the documented criticism (overkill for simple UIs, hard to generalise up front, large-scale binding performance). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model%E2%80%93view%E2%80%93viewmodel

John Gossman, Model-View-ViewModel (2005), the origin account describing MVVM as a WPF/Avalon-oriented refinement of MVC with a view-specific model, data binding and commands. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/johngossman/model-view-viewmodel

Microsoft Learn, Data binding and MVVM - .NET MAUI: XAML BindingContext view-models, one-way/two-way bindings and ICommand actions in a cross-platform UI stack. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/maui/xaml/fundamentals/mvvm?view=net-maui-10.0

Android Developers, UI State production: ViewModel-backed StateFlow or Compose State, lifecycle-aware collection and unidirectional UI events for Jetpack Compose screens. https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/ui-layer/state-production

Apple Developer Documentation, Managing model data in your app: @Observable model data, @State ownership and Bindable bindings tracked by SwiftUI. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app

Dave M. Bush, 4 Reasons To Drop MVVM: a criticism arguing that two-way binding and automatic recalculation can impose performance, memory and complexity costs in non-trivial apps, so MVVM should be applied selectively. https://davembush.github.io/4-reasons-to-drop-mvvm/
